results.title: World Bank forecasts 23% commodity price surge in 2026, warns of oil, food shocks in 2027
results.description: Global commodity prices are expected to surge by 23 percent this year, driven by soaring energy costs and mounting disruptions to food supplies, with the World Bank warning that worsening conflicts and an unusually strong El Niño could trigger another wave of price increases in 2027. In the October 2026 edition of its biannual Commodity Markets Outlook report released on Wednesday night, Oct. 28 (Manila time), the World Bank Group (WBG) projected that commodity prices would reach their second-highest level since 2013, reversing three consecutive years of declines. The latest forecast represents a substantial upward revision from the Washington-based multilateral lender’s April projection of a 16-percent increase in commodity prices this year, reflecting prolonged disruptions from the Middle East conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war, and extreme weather conditions. Energy prices are forecast to jump by 32 percent in 2026, their highest level in four years, before declining by 11.5 percent in 2027 as supply conditions gradually improve. Brent crude oil prices are projected to average $91 per barrel this year, up from $69 in 2025, before easing to $79 in 2027. The latest oil price forecast is higher than the World Bank’s April projections of $86 per barrel for 2026 and $70 for 2027. However, the lender warned that a renewed escalation of hostilities in the Middle East, combined with continued disruptions to Russian oil production and exports, could push Brent prices to an average of $105 per barrel next year. “Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once,” World Bank deputy chief economist and prospects group director Ayhan Kose said in a statement. “Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth. The priority must be to protect the poorest people and support low-income countries already struggling with heavy debt burdens,” Kose said. The report showed that global oil production is expected to decline by 5.2 percent this year, the largest annual contraction in more than four decades outside the 2020 global recession. Global oil consumption is likewise projected to fall by 2.5 percent, marking the third-largest annual decline on record after 2020 and 1980, as higher prices and supply shortages curb demand. Despite weaker consumption, global oil production has remained below demand, forcing withdrawals from inventories averaging about 2.4 million barrels daily between March and September. The World Bank said Brent prices reached approximately $110 per barrel in mid-October, while prices of refined petroleum products, particularly diesel and jet fuel, rose even more sharply amid damage to refineries and disruptions to export routes. Natural gas markets have also faced significant pressure, with European natural gas prices projected to average $19 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) this year, up from $12 in 2025. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices in Japan, a benchmark for Asian markets, are forecast to climb to $20 per MMBtu from $12 last year before moderating to $18 in 2027. Meanwhile, food commodity prices are projected to increase by about 10 percent in 2026 and another seven percent in 2027, representing a cumulative rise of approximately 18 percent over the two years. The World Bank attributed the increases to disruptions in Black Sea grain shipments, higher energy and agricultural input costs, and the effects of a very strong El Niño on crop production. Grain prices are expected to rise by 14 percent this year and another nine percent in 2027, with adverse weather conditions threatening rice production in Asia and wheat harvests globally. The lender projected that the international benchmark price of Thai rice with five-percent broken grains would increase from $408 per metric ton (MT) in 2025 to $448 this year and $500 in 2027. Wheat prices are likewise forecast to climb from $243 per MT last year to $311 this year and $353 in 2027, while maize prices are projected to increase from $203 to $223 and $235 over the same period. Fertilizer prices are expected to rise by 14 percent in 2026, reflecting earlier increases in urea prices and higher production costs, before declining by 12 percent next year. The World Bank warned that simultaneous disruptions to energy supplies, Black Sea grain shipments, and agricultural production from an unusually powerful El Niño could push food prices above their 2022 levels in an adverse scenario. Beyond energy and agriculture, metals and minerals prices are projected to increase by approximately 25 percent this year, reaching record levels amid strong demand from renewable energy (RE), electric vehicles (EVs), data centers, and other technology-related investments. Copper prices are forecast to average $13,200 per MT in 2026, up from $9,947 last year, while nickel prices are expected to rise to $17,200 from $15,162. Tin prices are projected to surge to $51,000 per MT from $34,059, while aluminum prices are expected to climb to $3,250 from $2,632. Precious metals prices are also forecast to increase by about 40 percent this year, supported by demand for safe-haven assets amid geopolitical and economic uncertainty. Gold prices are projected to average $4,600 per troy ounce in 2026, compared with $3,442 last year, while silver prices are expected to rise to $70 from $39.80. The World Bank expects overall commodity prices to decline by seven percent in 2027 and another nine percent in 2028, although the outlook depends on easing geopolitical tensions, recovering energy supplies, and manageable agricultural losses. To help countries manage the impact of rising prices, the WBG said it has made $50 billion to $60 billion available through existing financing instruments, including $25 billion in prearranged financing, to support social safety nets, fiscal capacity, and working capital for businesses and farms.

results.title: Identical twins showed a survival divide when only one had Parkinson’s
results.description: Researchers followed 54 twin pairs discordant for Parkinson’s disease and found substantially higher 10-year mortality among affected twins, including in genetically identical pairs. They also observed more frequent constipation among affected twins, but dietary and nutritional differences were limited, with secondary findings requiring confirmation.
